0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

The implication is that Saul sent men to watch David’s house in order to kill him, as recorded in 1 Samuel 19:11. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When Saul sent men to watch David’s house to kill him]

1.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates an urgent request to God rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an urgent request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please set me on high] or [I beg you to set me on high]

David is speaking of protection as if Yahweh could **Set** him **on high** in an unreachable place above his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Keep me safe from them] or [Put me beyond their reach]
The pronoun **ones** refers to David’s enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [away from the enemies rising up against me]

2.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please deliver me]

David is using the possessive form to describe **workers** who are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from people who do wicked things] or [from those who practice evil]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from people who do evil things]

This is an imperative, but it communicates an urgent request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates an urgent request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please save me]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **men** who are characterized by **blood**. This refers to people who are violent or who commit murder. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and save me from violent men] or [and save me from murderers]

Here, **blood** represents violence and murder. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and save me from violent men] or [and save me from murderous men]

3.note: The psalmist is using **behold** as a common expression to draw the reader’s attention to what he is about to say. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [notice] or [see]

Here, **life** represents the whole person as the target of an attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to attack me] or [to murder me]

David is using the adjective **mighty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [mighty men] or [very strong men]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [They gather against me not for my transgression and not for my sin] or [This is happening not for my transgression and not for my sin]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I transgressed against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because I have sinned]

4.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [though I have done nothing wrong]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were asleep and needed to **Awake**. David means that he wants Yahweh to take action and help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or you could express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come to meet me]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that would be used to make a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please awaken]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [and please look at my situation]

5.note: The expression **God of armies** refers to Yahweh as the commander of the heavenly armies, meaning the angelic hosts. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [God who rules over the angelic hosts]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please arise to punish] or [I beg you to arise and punish]

The psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were asleep and needed to **wake up**. He means that he wants Yahweh to begin to intervene and punish the nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [come and act]

David says **all of the nations** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [the hostile nations] or [these enemy nations]

The word translated as **Do not be gracious** is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please do not show favor] or [I beg you not to be gracious]

David is using the possessive form to describe **workers** who are characterized by **iniquity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people who are treacherous and who do wicked things] or [treacherous people who do evil]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

6.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies introduced in verses 1–3. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The psalmist’s enemies return]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dog** is threatening and aggressive, so are the psalmist’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they make threatening sounds] or [they snarl aggressively]

By **go around the city**, the psalmist means that David’s enemies are roaming around Jerusalem looking for victims. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [roam around the city looking for prey] or [prowl around the city seeking victims]

7.note: The psalmist is using **Behold** as a common expression to draw attention to what follows. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look] or [Pay attention]

The psalmist is using **they belch out with their mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean that his enemies speak violently or arrogantly. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they speak violent threats] or [they pour out arrogant words]

The psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ words as if they were **swords** that could physically harm people. This image emphasizes how dangerous and hurtful their speech is. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their lips speak harmful words] or [their words are as dangerous as swords]

Here, **lips** represents speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in their speech] or [in what they say]

The psalmist’s enemies are using the question form for emphasis. They assume that no one hears or cares what they say. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one is hearing] or [No one hears us!]

8.note: The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the threats of his enemies and God’s response to them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You, however, Yahweh] or [You, Yahweh, on the other hand]

The psalmist is using **laugh at them** as a common expression of the culture to mean “scorn them” or “treat them with contempt.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [ridicule them] or [look upon them with contempt]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [But you, Yahweh, laugh at them, indeed, you mock all of the nations]

9.note: The pronoun **his** may refer to God, but some Hebrew manuscripts and many translations understand it as **my**. This would make the psalmist say that God is **my strength**, which fits better with the context where he calls God **my stronghold**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could clarify this. Alternate translation: [my strength] or [you, my strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who are strong] or [you who strengthen me]

The psalmist is speaking of God as if he were a **stronghold**, that is, a fortified place of safety. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God protects me] or [God is my place of safety]

10.note: David is using the possessive form to describe **the God** who is characterized by **covenant faithfulness** toward him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God, who is faithful to his covenant with me] or [God, who keeps his covenant promises to me]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who is faithfully loyal to me in his covenant] or [who faithfully keeps his covenant with me]

The psalmist is using **will make me look upon my enemies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “will cause me to see my enemies defeated” or “will enable me to see my enemies humiliated.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will let me see my enemies defeated] or [will enable me to see myself humiliating my enemies]

11.note: The expression translated as **Do not slay them** is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [Please do not kill them] or [I ask that you not kill them]

David is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives God an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [so that my people will not forget] or [because if you do, my people will forget]

Here David is using the pronoun **my** with **people** to refer to the nation of Israel, over whom he reigns as king. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites] or [the people of Israel]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a request to God rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a request to God. It may be helpful to use a word such as “please.” Alternate translation: [Please scatter them] or [We ask that you scatter them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are powerful]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please bring them down] or [I ask you to humble them]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shield** that protects the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our protector]

12.note: David is using the possessive form to describe a **sin** that is characterized by **their mouth**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sin characterized by their mouth] or [the sin that comes from their mouth]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sin**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [For what they say that is sinful] or [For the sinful words]

Here the phrases **their mouth** and **their lips** represent what the psalmist’s enemies say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what they say] or [their spoken words]

The expression **may they be taken in their pride** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [may their pride trap them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because they are proud]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the curse**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how they curse people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lying**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and for the untruthful stories]

13.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a request rather than a command for God to destroy his enemies. If the imperative does not communicate a request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a request. Alternate translation: [I ask that you consume them in wrath] or [Please consume them in wrath]

The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **Consume** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Completely consume them in wrath]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are angered] or [wrathfully]

David is using the phrase **that they may not be** to introduce the goal or purpose of consuming his enemies in wrath. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that they will no longer exist] or [in order that they will be destroyed]

Here, **that they may know** marks **that God is ruling in Jacob to the ends of the earth** as a further goal or purpose of **Consume them in wrath; consume them that they may not be**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that people may know] or [in order that all may know]

Here, **Jacob** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [over Israel] or [the people of Israel]

The phrase **to the ends of the earth** was a common expression meaning “everywhere” or “throughout the entire world.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere] or [throughout the whole world]

The word **Selah** is a Hebrew word. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote.

14.note: This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [In the evening they return]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dog** growls when it is threatening or angry, so the psalmist’s enemies make threatening sounds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they make threatening sounds like an angry dog]

15.note: Here the psalmist is stating the pronoun **They** separately, even though the verb translated as **they wander** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between him and his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here.

David is speaking as if this were a hypothetical possibility, but he means that it is actually true. If your language does not state something as a condition if it is certain or true, or if your readers might think that what David is saying is uncertain, then you could translate this as a confident statement. Alternate translation: [When they are not full, they lodge]

16.note: Here David is using the pronoun **I** twice for emphasis. He is doing this to contrast his response to God with the actions of his enemies, which he described earlier in the psalm. If a speaker of your language would repeat a pronoun in this way for emphasis, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing this emphasis. Alternate translation: [But as for me, I]

David uses the words **But I** here to indicate a strong contrast between the enemies described in the previous verses and himself. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [As for me, however, I] or [In contrast to them, I]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how strong you are]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about how you are faithful to your covenant] or [about how faithful you are to me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **stronghold** that protected him from enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable figure of speech or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are like a fortified place to me]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **a refuge** in which he could find safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and a place of safety]

David is using **in the day of trouble** as a common expression to mean “when I am in trouble.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when I am in trouble] or [in times of distress]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trouble**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when I am troubled] or [when I experience troubles]

17.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [you who make me strong] or [you who strengthen me]

David is speaking of God as if he were a **stronghold**, a fortified place where David could be protected from his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent metaphor from your culture. Alternatively, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [God protects me] or [God keeps me safe from my enemies]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the God who is faithful to his covenant]
